items.abstract: <jats:p>Instantaneous local Gaussian approximations assign nuclear momentum widths from the curvature of the potential at each sampled configuration. Strongly compressed bonds can consequently acquire large momentum widths even when their positions are drawn from an anharmonic path-integral ensemble. We estimate momentum covariances from pathintegral coordinates and forces in local modes that follow molecular deformations. These covariances define Gaussian approximations to high-frequency Wigner momentum marginals without evaluating a Hessian at each configuration. The resulting sampling recovers the Maxwell momentum distribution in the classical limit. A rotating bond model with harmonic stretching and periodic torsion agrees with an independent quantum reference within statistical uncertainty. For trans-azobenzene at 300 K with 32 beads, the most compressed C–H bond receives a mass-weighted momentum variance of 36.53 kJ mol−1 from LGA and 19.55 kJ mol−1 from the local covariance along the same physical stretch direction. Temporal holdout errors in C–H second moments are 7.2–7.6%, compared with 2.2–5.1% for LGA relative to the finite-bead reference; the demonstrated benefit concerns the suppression of local width spikes. The largest collective C–H width remains sensitive to estimator noise. These results support the method as an approximation to high-frequency momentum widths without a frequency cap. Position-conditioned quantum correlations, non-Gaussian tails, and the continuum-bead molecular limit remain outside the demonstrated accuracy.</jats:p>
title: Wigner Momentum Estimation and Sampling with Local Modes: A Second-Moment Approximation to High-Frequency Momentum Marginals

items.abstract: <jats:p>Medium-sized aliphatic rings are underrepresented in drug discovery despite their advantageous balance of rigidity and flexibility. Existing synthetic limitations hinder broader exploration of this valuable chemical space. This work presents a general and efficient method for the one- and two-carbon ring expansion of 5- and 6-membered allylic alcohols to larger cyclic ketones using cerium-based photoredox catalysis. Employing ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) activation, a dual catalytic system featuring Ce(OTf)3 and 9,10-diphenylanthracene (DPA) enables selective generation of alkoxyl radicals under mild conditions. A hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) catalyst, (TRIPS)2, is critical for productive C–C bond formation and radical termination. The method tolerates various nitrogen-protecting groups, vinyl substitutions, and ring systems, including bridged and fused frameworks, affording 7- and 8-membered ketones in moderate to excellent yields (38–98%). Notably, expansion to challenging [5.2.1] bicyclic and fused benzannulated scaffolds is demonstrated. This strategy offers a divergent and synthetically accessible route to sp3-rich, conformationally diverse drug-like scaffolds from simple precursors.</jats:p>
title: Cerium Photoredox-Catalyzed Ring Expansion of Cyclic Allylic Alcohols

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                  Liquid chromatography (LC) is the analytical workhorse of pharmaceutical research and, at the same time, one of its largest sources of organic solvent waste and energy consumption. High-throughput experimentation amplifies this burden by generating thousands of samples per campaign, each conventionally analyzed by methods that consume milliliters to liters of solvent per system and keep instruments running for hours. Because solvent consumption and instrument energy demand scale directly with run time, accelerating these analyses is both a throughput and a sustainability priority. Routine implementation of ultrafast LC, however, has been limited by two related barriers: the experimental effort required to identify high-speed conditions that retain decision-critical selectivity, and the solvent-intensive nature of method development itself. Herein, we introduce a predictive
                  <jats:italic toggle="yes">in silico</jats:italic>
                  framework that transforms ultrafast LC assay development from empirical screening into a model-driven design workflow. Experimental retention data are used to model chromatographic selectivity across temperature, gradient slope, flow rate, and column geometry, enabling rapid identification of the fastest separation conditions that preserve the information required for decision-making. Retention modeling is further combined with fit-for-purpose resolution criteria and
                  <jats:italic toggle="yes">in silico</jats:italic>
                  peak clustering to selectively resolve critical components while intentionally grouping noncritical analytes to maximize throughput. The approach is demonstrated across closely related isomers, chiral analyses, and high-throughput reaction screening, where model-predicted separations translated directly into reliable experiments, substantially shortened analysis cycle times, and required minimal manual intervention. The resulting methods give lower analytical method greenness scores, in some cases by more than 10-fold. Together, this framework establishes a general strategy for systematically deploying greener ultrafast chromatographic assays while reducing method-development burden, solvent consumption, and energy demand, with broad applicability to biocatalysis, natural products, metabolomics, high-throughput experimentation, and modern synthesis.
                </jats:p>
title: Predictive Design of Greener Ultrafast Chromatography for Accelerated Discovery and Development Chemistry

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                  The acid-catalyzed dehydration of D-(−)-fructose into 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) and side product levulinic acid (LA) in saturated aqueous sodium chloride was investigated with
                  <jats:sup>1</jats:sup>
                  H quantitative nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (qNMR) and micellar capillary electrokinetic chromatography (MEKC). The highest isolated HMF yield of 32.7 ± 5.4 % was obtained with 2 mol% sulfonated calix[4]arene (sC4A) from 0.3 M fructose over 4 hours at 140 °C showing modestly improved performance over
                  <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                  -toluenesulfonic acid, methanesulfonic acid, p-hydroxybenzenesulfonic acid, sulfuric acid and hydrochloric acid. Host-guest interactions between sC4A and HMF were investigated with
                  <jats:sup>1</jats:sup>
                  H NMR titrations at different temperatures revealing supramolecular complexation at 30 °C, whereas
                  <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                  -hydroxybenzenesulfonic acid bearing same functional groups but lacking the macrocyclic cavity of sC4A did not show interactions with HMF. A MECK method for the HMF analysis from acidic reaction mixtures was developed reaching limit of detection and limit of quantification values of 0.003 mM and 0.009 mM, respectively. Here we demonstrate that MEKC can be used to track the production of HMF at the concentration range 0.1–10 mM within a total analysis time of 2 minutes.
                </jats:p>
title: Synthesis of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural using sulfonated calix[4]arene in brine and rapid reaction monitoring with micellar capillary electrokinetic chromatography

items.abstract: <jats:p>A dioxasilepane-derived styrenic monomer, 2,4,4,7,7-pentamethyl-2-(4-vinylphenyl)-1,3,2-dioxasilepane (St-Si(pan)Me), is introduced as the first polymerizable representative of the recently developed Si(pan) platform, a seven-membered cyclic dialkoxysilane motif combining high stability with controllable silicon reactivity. The monomer combines the exceptional kinetic stability of the seven-membered cyclic dialkoxysilane with a polymerizable styrenic functionality, enabling direct incorporation of the Si(pan) motif into polystyrene-based polymers and materials. Following multigram-scale synthesis, the compatibility of St-Si(pan)Me with conventional free-radical polymerization was systematically investigated. Among the investigated polymerization temperatures (70 - 90 °C), 90 °C provided the best balance between molar-mass distribution, structural fidelity, thermal stability, and photophysical performance while fully preserving the integrity of the Si(pan) framework. Beyond free radical polymerization, Reversible Addition-Fragmentation Chain-Transfer (RAFT) polymerization showed compatibility with controlled radical polymerization, while preliminary emulsion polymerization revealed distinct behavior under aqueous conditions, suggesting opportunities for future siloxane network formation. Copolymerization with styrene afforded silicon-functionalized copolymers with tuneable compositions and systematically adjustable molecular, thermal, and photophysical properties. Comprehensive characterization by various techniques confirmed successful incorporation of the Si(pan) functionality throughout the polymer series. This work establishes St-Si(pan)Me as a versatile platform monomer that expands the toolbox of silicon-functionalized styrenes and provides access to a new class of thermally robust and intrinsically luminescent silicon-containing polystyrenes.</jats:p>
title: A Dioxasilepane-Functionalized Styrenic Monomer as a Platform for Novel Silicon-Containing Polystyrenes
